take.en: A headless 3D and VFX engine built for agents — they write the scene as code, render on GPU, inspect the frame, and revise. No editor to drive.

why.en: Most creative stacks still assume a human in Blender or After Effects. vork flips that: agents own the shot loop end to end, so product teams can ship real rendered 3D and VFX without a video model or a timeline UI.

explanation.en: vork is Voyager’s rendering kernel: Rust plus Slang on Vulkan or Metal, free during the research preview. There is no GUI. An agent (or you) authors a scene, calls render, looks at the PNG or MP4, then edits the program. Ordinary shots are scene JSON; weird shots get GPU programs for materials, light paths, simulation, and compositing. Examples go from a first sphere to a million-bird murmuration, VFX over real footage, and a black-hole lensing shot — none of that is generative video.

howItWorks.en: Install the release for Linux/Windows NVIDIA or Apple Silicon Metal, then paste a short prompt to your coding agent: read vork help, make a small scene, render a preview, refine camera and light, then final. Save scene JSON (Python and TypeScript SDKs ship in the install folder), run vork render shot.json --profile std/previs, inspect the image, and loop. Frame ranges mux to MP4 when you need a clip.

different.en: Blender and Nuke expose knobs for people. vork keeps the thin kernel agents cannot invent on the fly — geometry, ray queries, GPU time — and lets the agent write the rest as code mid-shot. That is the opposite of OpenMontage-style edit pipelines and rea-video-style reverse engineering: this is forward production for agent drivers.
